UX case study · Desktop web · 2021

Five tools down to one: designing the store admin for a gaming rewards platform

Lootline* runs online stores where gamers buy and redeem game credits, gift cards and merch. I designed the admin portal its team uses to run those stores: products, orders, partners, suppliers, users and reports.

Role
Product designer, the only designer on the project
Team
Me, a business analyst, the client's store team and the engineers
Scope
Release 1.0 · 13 modules · 260+ screens and states
Tools
Figma, shared component library

*Not the real name. The client is a gaming and esports media company; I worked on this through a product studio.

01

Project overview

Running the store meant jumping between five tools. Only technical staff could change the catalogue, and no single screen showed how the store was doing.

Lootline sells through partners, the brands whose players shop in the store, and buys from suppliers, the top-up and voucher providers who deliver each order. Partner and supplier staff also needed their own access. The brief was a single back office that a non-technical store team could use every day, with the right permissions for everyone else.

ProductAdmin portal for a game credits and rewards store
UsersStore admins, partner admins, supplier admins, view-only staff
My workDiscovery, information architecture, flows, component library, hi-fi screens and every state, developer handoff
MethodsWalkthrough of the current setup · tool audit · requirement sessions · role mapping · flows · component library
Problem

Orders arrived as raw notification emails. Prices lived in a spreadsheet, reports in a separate BI tool, and products in a developer admin panel.

Goal

One portal to manage the catalogue, handle and refund orders, onboard partners and suppliers, control access and read the numbers.

02

Exploration & discovery

Method A

Walkthrough of the current setup

Why

Before drawing anything I needed to see how the store was run day to day. A requirements document says what a system should do. It doesn't show the copying and pasting people do to get through the day.

What I found

A single order touched five tools. An email alert carried raw item and user IDs and a link into a developer admin panel. Someone then bought the item on a supplier's website and checked prices in a shared spreadsheet. Sales numbers sat in a separate BI report.

What it changed

Every step that crossed from one tool to another became part of the portal. Orders, catalogue, suppliers and reports had to live behind one sign-in and use the same IDs.

1Store admin portalone sign-in · one set of IDs · roles for every user type

Frames from the walkthrough recordings, blurred on purpose: only the shape of the old workflow matters here.

Method B

Requirement sessions → a module map

Why

The business analyst owned the requirements. Turning them into a module map before any screens gave us one shared picture to agree on and to cut scope against.

What I found

Nine modules. Products, partners, suppliers and users were all the same kind of job: find a record, check its status, add or edit it, and act on several at once.

What it changed

I designed one list pattern and one add/edit pattern and reused them across modules. That decision shaped the whole product.

Store admin
DashboardOverview · widgets
ReportsOverview · products · orders · partners · suppliers
ProductsAll products · categories · attributes
OrdersAll orders · receipts · refunds
PartnersGeneral · agreements · account mgmt
SuppliersGeneral · integration
UsersActive · invited · roles
HelpGuides
SettingsGeneral · notifications · theme · time zone · currency · privacy · role permissions
Shared list patternStatus tabs → filter + search → table → row menu → bulk actions → pagination
Shared add/edit patternVertical section tabs → outlined form fields → sticky footer: secondary action, Back, Next/Save
Method C

Role & permission mapping

Why

The portal wasn't only for the client's team. Partner and supplier staff needed to sign in too, and each should see only their part.

What I found

Five kinds of user: superadmin, administrator, partner administrator, supplier administrator and view-only. A plain "admin or not" switch couldn't cover them.

What it changed

Permissions became a tree. Each module has sections, and each section has view, edit, add and delete. Every invite is tied to a role, and invites stay visible until they're accepted or cancelled.

SuperadminAdministratorPartner administratorSupplier administratorView only
Products
View products
Edit products
Add new products
Delete products

What discovery boiled down to

  1. One pattern per job. Every list and every form works the same way, so the team learns the portal once.
  2. Status first. Published, unpublished and trashed; completed, processing, cancelled and refunded. Status is the first filter, shown as tabs and chips.
  3. Safe by default. Undo after risky actions, guard rails on bulk actions and locked fields that shouldn't change.
03

UX design process

Key flows

I mapped the three flows the store team would run most often before designing their screens. Each one replaced a hand-off between two of the old tools.

Add a product

  1. Pick supplier
  2. Product details
  3. Attributes
  4. Publish or save unpublished

Connect a supplier

  1. General info
  2. Endpoint + auth type
  3. Test connection
  4. Choose their products

Handle an order

  1. Filter by type / status
  2. Open receipt
  3. Check gamer account
  4. Complete, cancel or refund

A component library first

With 260+ screens and several modules repeating the same patterns, I built the library before the screens. It has a type scale from 10 to 32 px in four weights, buttons in every state, outlined form fields with hint, error and locked states, and toast messages.

Versions that didn't hold up

The designs below are the ones that changed most between their first and final versions. Here's what didn't work in each first version and what I changed.

Iteration 1

Dashboard: from a fixed report to a board you arrange

What was wrong. A store admin, a partner admin and a finance viewer care about different numbers. A fixed layout either buried someone's numbers or showed everyone everything.

What I changed. An edit mode with a remove link on every widget and an Add widgets picker. Below the charts, a cards/tabs toggle lets people keep the long tables collapsed.

Iteration 2

Role permissions: from a modal to a full page

What was wrong. The permission tree goes three levels deep: module, section, action. Inside a modal it needed its own scrollbar on top of the page's. You lost your place, and Save sat far from the item you'd just changed.

What I changed. A full page that scrolls once. Name and display name sit at the top, and the footer with Cancel and Save changes stays fixed. Select all, Unselect all and Reset to default handle bulk changes.

Iteration 3

Duplicate confirmation: name the ID, not the title

What was wrong. Product titles are long and nearly identical ("… 8100 UC", "… 3850 UC"). A toast that repeats the title doesn't tell you which product was copied, and the copy shows up as "Copy – …" truncated in the table.

What I changed. The toast names the product ID, which is short and unique, and keeps Undo on the right. That ID is the same one shown in the table, the receipt and supplier mapping.

04

Final design

A single portal where every module reads the same way, so a store admin who learns Products already knows Orders, Partners and Users.

Why this solution. The store team weren't developers. They needed status at a glance, safe bulk actions and forms that explain themselves. Hint text, character limits and "What can I upload?" helpers all serve that.

What else was on the table. Adding missing pages to the existing developer admin would have been faster to build. But it was designed around database tables and raw IDs, not store tasks. I also chose vertical section tabs over a strict wizard for products, partners and suppliers. That way, editing a published record can jump straight to the section that needs fixing.

Dashboard

Profit and overview cards up top, then a weekly or yearly chart with tabs for sales, cost, revenue, stocks, products and orders. Top partners and suppliers sit side by side, followed by top sellers by region.

The long tables (top products, partners, suppliers) each link straight into their module with an add button.

Scroll inside the frame to see the whole page →

Reports

The dashboard's charts, made printable and downloadable. Colour-coded KPI cards show change, and there are separate reports for products, orders, partners and suppliers.

Every report has a loading state designed. Waiting for numbers shouldn't look like broken numbers.

05

Impact

I don't have post-launch numbers I can share, so I won't quote any. Here's what was delivered and how I'd judge whether it worked.

What shipped to engineering

1portal replacing five tools in the order workflow
13module pages in the Release 1.0 developer file
260+desktop screens and states, including loading, error, empty and undo
5user roles with a permission tree per module

What I'd measure

  • Time to fulfil an order, from alert to completed, compared with the email-and-supplier-site routine
  • Catalogue changes by non-technical staff: how many product edits no longer need a developer
  • Refund and cancel handling time from the receipt view
  • Tools opened per order. The target is one.
06

Learnings

Watch the work before reading the spec

The walkthrough recordings explained the real job better than any requirement line. Five tools for one order was the whole case for the product, and no document said it.

Patterns beat pages

Once the list and add/edit patterns were solid, each new module was mostly content. It also made the portal easier to learn and easier for engineers to build.

Design the states, not just the screens

Loading reports, a blocked bulk action, a refunded receipt and a wrong verification code are where a back office earns trust. They took as long as the happy paths.

What I'd do differently

I'd run a copy review before handoff. Going back through the file, typos had slipped into labels, such as "Prodoucts", "Intergration" and "Genrel overview". I'd also put a clickable prototype in front of the store team earlier.
